Socrates. Four hundred and sixty-nine to three hundred and ninety-nine BCE. He was an Athenian philosopher who revolutionized Western thought by turning away from natural philosophy toward ethics and the examined life. He left no writings, but his method—eliciting truth through dialogue and exposing contradiction—shaped Plato and centuries of philosophy. His trial and execution by Athens became philosophy's defining image of the martyr for truth.

We know Socrates through dialogues written by his students, chiefly Plato and Xenophon. He wandered Athens engaging anyone—politicians, poets, craftsmen—in conversation, questioning their assumptions. His method was to pretend ignorance, ask probing questions, expose contradictions in what they claimed to know, and lead them toward truth. He claimed to know nothing. "I know that I know nothing," he said. He treated wisdom as recognition of one's own ignorance.

He rejected the natural philosophers' concerns. Instead he focused on ethical inquiry. How should one live? He believed that virtue is knowledge. Wrongdoing, he argued, stems from ignorance, not malice. Virtue cannot be taught in the ordinary sense, but it is discovered through dialogue and self-examination. He held that the soul is immortal and that moral integrity is more valuable than life itself.

In three hundred and ninety-nine BCE, Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting youth. He was tried before an Athenian court. He refused to flee or recant his beliefs. He drank hemlock and died calmly, becoming philosophy's martyr-hero. Never wrote anything himself. All knowledge of him comes from Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes, and Aristotle.

Socrates represents the birth of moral philosophy in the Western tradition. His refusal to reduce truth to received opinion or conventional piety, and his willingness to die for intellectual integrity, made him the archetype of the philosopher as truth-seeker and ethical exemplar. The Socratic method remains central to education and philosophical practice. His influence flows through Plato into Aristotle, and forward into every school that values questions over dogma.
